1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5.name: Grünfeld Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5.background: Ernst Grünfeld brought the defence into international play at Bad Pistyan in 1922, drawing Friedrich Sämisch in his first game with it, and later that year beat Alexander Alekhine in Vienna.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn and clears the way for e4: White builds a broad pawn centre, and Black attacks it with pieces and pressure on the long diagonal. The game turns on whether the centre is a strength or an overextended target. The main battleground of the Grünfeld.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5.name: Grünfeld Defence: Stockholm Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop before committing to a centre. Black usually answers with the knight to e4, hitting the bishop and offering a trade that often leaves White with doubled c-pawns. The resulting positions are balanced.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3.name: Grünfeld Defence: Lutikov Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 to build a broad pawn centre without allowing the knight exchange on c3. It takes f3 from the g1 knight and loosens the king's position, so Black must strike at the centre soon, but White keeps a slight edge in the main line.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4.name: Grünfeld Defence: Brinckmann Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4.background: Considered a safer choice than the Exchange Variation, it has declined significantly since its heyday in the 1930s and is not often met in top-flight play today.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before e3. White goes for queenside initiative with a smaller pawn centre, rather than a big centre for Black to attack.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and holds the centre together, a more conservative way to meet the Grünfeld than the Exchange. White keeps the pawn centre and waits for Black's break, so the game is slower and Black's counterplay is adequate.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Qb3.name: Grünfeld Defence: Russian Variation, Accelerated Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Qb3.strategy: An early queen move that defends c4 and holds the option of recapturing there. White gets a centre by taking on c4 and playing e4, but the queen comes out early, and Black may gain time by developing with a hit on it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3.strategy: A modest reply: the pawn supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop, but White gives up the idea of a broad centre and leaves Black free to strike at it. Safe, but it hands Black an easy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.g4.name: Grünfeld Defence: Gibbon Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.g4.strategy: A pawn offered at once: the g4 pawn is attacked by both the c8 bishop and the f6 knight and nothing defends it, so Black simply takes it. White would need a lot of activity in return to justify the loss.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.h4.name: Grünfeld Defence: Zaitsev Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.h4.strategy: A flank attack in the Grünfeld that ignores the centre: the c4 pawn is attacked by the d5 pawn and nothing defends it, so Black simply takes it. White hopes to open the kingside with h5, but the pawn is lost first.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and prepares castling. The bishop on f4 is ignored for now, since the queen guards c7, and the bishop on g7 will bear down on d4 and the queenside once the f6 knight steps aside. Black develops first and counterattacks the centre next.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once and gives up the central tension. White regains it with Qa4+ and Qxc4, or with e3 and Bxc4, while the bishop on f4 stays active, so Black has mostly spent time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 c6.strategy: Backs d5 with a pawn, so cxd5 can be recaptured with a pawn and the centre stays solid. The cost is a tempo and some of the Grünfeld's bite: Black no longer hits the centre with pieces at once, and White develops freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and the bishop on f4, and opens the f1-bishop to guard c4. White plays for the initiative on the queenside with a smaller, safer pawn centre rather than the big one that cxd5 and e4 would build.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.Rc.strategy: Brings the rook to the c-file at once, but leaves c4 unprotected: the f1-bishop is still shut in by the e2 pawn, so Black may simply take on c4 and White has to justify the pawn. Black can also castle and let White play e3 next.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the knight toward the centre, supporting d4 and covering e5, and keeps the choice between a quiet e3 and an early e4 for later. Black can take on c4, but White can usually regain the pawn with e3 or Qa4+, so the game stays flexible.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e3.name: Grünfeld Defence: Brinckmann Attack, Grünfeld Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e3.strategy: Castles and lets the centre tension stand. If White takes on d5, the queen's recapture later leaves the c7 pawn to fall, but Black gets quick development and pressure on d4 in return. A gambit that asks White to accept it, instead of the more usual immediate counter-strike in the centre.

Strikes at d4 at once, before White has finished developing, the Grünfeld's usual answer to a pawn centre. If White takes on c5, Black's queen and pieces gain active play against the c3 knight and the queenside; if White holds d4, the bishop on g7 gets its diagonal.
Takes the pawn, but with e3 played White regains it at once with Bxc4, a developing move. Black has released the central tension for nothing, and White's bishop settles on an active diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e3.name: Grünfeld Defence: Brinckmann Attack, Grünfeld Gambit, Capablanca Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e3.strategy: Declines the gambit and puts the rook on the c-file, where it will look down the file when the position opens. White keeps the bishop on f4 and the pawn on e3 solid and avoids the sharp line in which Black's pieces come alive for the pawn on c7.

Accepts the gambit. After the trades on d5 the queen recaptures and c7 hangs, so White wins a pawn. In return Black develops with tempo and pushes against the d4 pawn, so White has to defend accurately rather than attack.

Declines the gambit by backing the pawn on c4 and pressing on b7, while the bishop on f4 and the d4 and e3 pawns stay solid. The queen comes out early, though, and Black can strike at the centre without delay.

The natural recapture: the knight reaches the centre and attacks both the bishop on f4 and the knight on c3. Black accepts that a queen recapture on d5 will leave c7 unguarded: that is the pawn Black has offered.
A pawn sacrifice the position does not call for: after dxc6 Nxc6 the knight is developed, but Black is a pawn down and White's centre is intact.
Hangs the queen to Nxd5: Black can recapture only a knight, so the queen goes for a knight.

The standard counter-strike: Black hits d4 at once, before White has settled. If White takes on c5, the position opens and Black's pieces get active play against the c3 knight; if White holds d4, Black can trade the central pawn and free the bishop on g7.

Takes the pawn, which White regains at once with Bxc4, a developing move that also eyes f7. Black has released the central tension without winning anything and has given up the pressure on White's centre.

Backs d5 and keeps the structure compact, so cxd5 can be met by a pawn recapture. The cost is counterplay: Black is slower to challenge the centre, and White develops freely with the rook already on the c-file.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.Rc.strategy: Castles before anything else. The king is safe whichever way the centre is settled, and Black does not need to take the loose c4 pawn to be comfortable: White's e3 will close the gap and bring the same quiet set-up as with e3 first.
Takes the pawn that Rc1 left loose. White regains it at once with Qa4+ and Qxc4, or with e3 and Bxc4, so Black gains little beyond a brief extra pawn and has released the central tension.

Keeps the centre compact with a pawn on c6, so cxd5 can be met by ...cxd5. It spends a move on structure while the king is still in the centre, and White's e3 then brings everything into order at leisure.

Closes the gap: the pawn supports d4 and the bishop on f4, and the f1-bishop at last guards the c4 pawn. White reaches the same quiet set-up as with e3 first, with the rook already placed on the c-file, and declines any sharp play.

Opens the position at once. After the trades on d5 White can take on c7, but with e3 still unplayed the d4 pawn has only the queen behind it, and Black takes it back with the queen and the g7 bishop, with equal play.

Develops a piece before dealing with c4. Black can take the pawn, and White regains it with e3 and Bxc4, so this is a sound but slightly slow route to the usual quiet set-up with the rook already on the c-file.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Ne4.strategy: Attacks the bishop and the c3 knight at once. Black challenges the pressure on d5 by offering to trade off the c3 knight that presses on it, and keeps the initiative in the centre: White must retreat the bishop or exchange pieces.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Bg7.strategy: Develops and covers f6 a second time, so Bxf6 would be recaptured with the bishop and not the e-pawn. A sound way to meet the bishop, but Black has not yet challenged it, and White is free to choose the pawn structure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn, but it is hard to keep: White regains it with e3 and Bxc4, or with Qa4+, and the bishop on g5 stays aimed at f6. Black has given up the d5 pawn's hold on the centre for little.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Ne4 5.Nx.strategy: Trades knights instead of retreating the bishop. The recapture ...dxe4 gives Black a pawn on e4 that gains space and cramps White's kingside; the pawn is also a target, but White has given up the knight that pressed on d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Ne4 5.Bh.strategy: Keeps the bishop on the board instead of trading it, and holds the diagonal toward e7. After the knight trade on c3 and ...dxc4 Black is a pawn up for the moment, but White keeps a sound centre and the pawn is hard to hold.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Ne4 5.Bf.strategy: Retreats the bishop to the other diagonal, where it controls e5 and eyes c7. White must be ready to take on c3 with the b-pawn after the knight trade, since Black can then take on c4 and White has to win the pawn back.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Ne4 5.Nx.strategy: The only sensible recapture, and a good one: the pawn takes space on e4, removes the pressure on d5, and cramps White's kingside development. The pawn is a point of tension, because White can attack it, so Black must keep it supported.
Takes a pawn but leaves the knight on e4 alone: Black is a whole piece down for a pawn, with no way to win it back.
Attacks the knight, but Black is already a piece down and White simply moves it to safety, keeping the extra piece.
Protects the bishop on g5 and the d4 pawn in one move, and clears the d1 square so that White can castle long. White develops calmly and plans to undermine the pawn on e4 rather than hurry.
Supports d4 and frees the f1-bishop, so the pawn centre holds without the queen's help. The bishop on g5 is left unprotected, though, and Black can gain a tempo by attacking it.

Undermines the cramping pawn on e4 at once. If Black takes on f3, the knight recaptures and protects the bishop on g5 while developing; the cost is a loosened kingside, which makes White's king the target if the position opens.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Ne4 5.Nx.name: Grünfeld Defence: Lundin Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Ne4 5.Nx.strategy: Strikes at d4 straight away: with the queen on d8 also looking at it, the pawn is attacked twice and defended only by the queen. White must resolve the centre now, while Black keeps the cramping pawn on e4.

Develops the bishop onto the long diagonal, where it joins the queen against d4, now attacked twice and held only by the queen. White has to defend it, for example by castling long, while Black prepares to castle and keeps the cramping pawn on e4.

Adds a second attacker to d4 and develops, but the knight can be hit by d5, which gains space with tempo and takes the pawn out of the line of fire. A sound second-rate try: Black has to move the knight again.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5.name: Grünfeld Defence: Exchange Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5.background: The most frequent continuation of the Grünfeld Defence.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: The natural recapture, and the Grünfeld bet: the knight steps into the centre and invites White to build a large pawn centre with e4. Black will attack that centre from the wings and the long diagonal instead of occupying it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 c6.strategy: A pawn sacrifice that Black does not need: after dxc6 Nxc6 the knight is developed, but Black is a pawn down with no clear compensation.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Hangs the queen to Nxd5: Black can recapture only a knight, so the queen goes for a knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..strategy: Kicks the knight and builds the broad pawn centre in one go, exactly what Black has invited. White gets space and the initiative, but must keep the centre together under attack, since the pawns on d4 and e4 become the targets.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..name: Grünfeld Defence: Exchange Variation, Nadanian Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..background: Named after Ashot Nadanian, who first played it in 1996. His analysis, published in volume 67 of Chess Informant, caused major ripples in the chess world.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..strategy: Puts the knight on the edge to control c5 and discourage ...c5, Black's usual way of attacking the centre. The knight loses time, but e4 then wins it back by driving the d5 knight away. A deliberate challenge to the usual plans.

Develops with a point: if Black takes on c3, the bishop recaptures, so White avoids the weakened pawn structure that bxc3 brings. The price is a smaller centre, a quieter way to fight for the initiative than the full pawn centre.
Takes the knight before it is driven away. White must recapture, which gives White the big centre but leaves a pawn on c3 that will be a long-term target, and Black's pieces aim at exactly that.

Retreats instead of trading, so the knight on c3 stays and White builds the big centre at leisure with a healthy pawn structure. Black's knight stands passively on b6, and counterplay against d4 and e4 has to be found elsewhere.
Goes back to f6, but e5 attacks it again with a gain of space and time. The knight must move once more, Black has lost tempi, and White's centre grows unopposed.

Recaptures with the b-pawn, completing the large centre of pawns on c3, d4 and e4. White gets space and a free hand for the pieces, at the cost of a weak c3 pawn and a lonely a-pawn, so the centre has to stay active.
Attacks the knight on c3 but does not recapture it: ...Nxe4 takes a pawn and attacks the queen, so White is a whole piece down for nothing.
Develops but ignores the knight on c3, which takes the queen: ...Nxd1 wins the queen for a knight.
Aims the bishop along the long diagonal at the d4 pawn, the base of the white centre, and prepares castling. Black attacks the centre from a distance, and more pressure from the pieces will follow.

Attacks the base of White's pawn centre at once. White's pieces are not yet out, so the centre has to be defended or resolved immediately, and the queen and the bishop coming to g7 add to the pressure on d4.
Attacks d4 with a piece early, but the knight can be hit by d5 or pinned by Bb5, which threatens Bxc6+ and doubled pawns. White gains time with the big centre while Black finds the knight a square.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3 Bg7.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares castling. White's quiet pawn move leaves the bishop on g7 free to bear down on d4 as soon as the knight moves, and Black can finish development before deciding how to strike at the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before developing, the defence's typical counter-blow. White's e-pawn has already spent a move reaching e3, so a later e4 costs a tempo, and a capture on c5 lets Black pin the c3 knight with the queen. The price is that Black's king stays in the centre a little longer.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with the c-pawn and chooses a solid pawn chain over the defence's usual strike at d4. Black's centre is safe and the game calm, but the counterplay the fianchetto promises is traded for safety, and White keeps the freer position.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3 Bg7 5.Qb3.strategy: Guards c4 again and eyes b7, planning to regain the pawn at once if Black takes on c4. But the queen comes out before the pieces and spends time, so Black gets a free hand to take the pawn and then complete development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight guards d4 and prepares castling, and White keeps every option in the centre open. With e3 and Nf3 in place the d4 pawn is hard to attack, so Black has to look for counterplay while White settles for a solid, slow game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3 Bg7 5.cxd.strategy: Resolves the tension in the centre and plans to chase the recapturing knight with e4. But White has already spent a move on e3, so building the broad centre costs an extra tempo, and Black is a move ahead of the usual exchange line.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3 Bg7 5.Qb3.strategy: Takes the pawn rather than defend d5 passively. White regains it, but the queen on b3 and the time spent give Black the chance to castle and complete development, with a healthy structure and a freer game.

Supports d5 with the c-pawn, so Black keeps the centre pawn without taking on c4 and stays solid. The cost is the defence's counterplay: with the pawn on c6 the strike at d4 with ...c5 is gone, the game turns quieter and White keeps more space.

Reinforces d5 from behind and keeps the pawn centre intact. But the pawn on e6 closes the diagonal of the c8-bishop, and Black's set-up is passive: White keeps pressing on d5 and b7 while Black has nothing active to put against it.
Regains the pawn with a developing move, and the bishop eyes f7 with the queen behind it on b3. White's pieces aim at the kingside; Black has to meet the pressure on f7 before anything else.

Regains the pawn with the queen and keeps the f1-bishop free to choose its square. The cost is that the queen stands in the open on c4, where Black can gain time by attacking it with a developing move, so White's development lags a little. Sound, and slightly slower than the recapture with the bishop.

Develops before recapturing, since the pawn on c4 cannot be held for long: the queen and the bishop both attack it and nothing defends it. White gets the knight out and keeps the choice of recapture, but gives Black a free move for development.

Castles and adds the rook and king as defenders of f7, the point at which the bishop and the queen are aimed. Black's development is level, and Black can now play against d4 and the white queenside with the king safe.

Blocks the bishop's diagonal to f7 with a pawn instead of defending the pawn it attacks. That meets the threat, but the pawn on e6 shuts in the c8-bishop and Black stays cramped while White develops freely.

Guards f7 with the queen, so the king can wait in the centre. But the queen on d7 blocks the c8-bishop and the d-file, and White can harass it with a developing move, so Black loses time and the king still has to castle.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once, before the pawn on f3 can support an e4 centre. The pawn on d4 is defended only by the queen, so White must decide the centre now, while f3 has weakened the king's diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 Bg7.strategy: Develops the bishop but lets White take the broad centre it wants: e4 is supported by the pawn on f3, and e5 then drives the f6 knight back with gain of space. Black still has the strike at d4 in hand, yet White keeps a slight edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 dxc4.strategy: Grabs the pawn, but White simply builds the centre with e4, which the pawn on f3 supports, and soon regains the pawn or keeps a lead in space for it. Black is left defending rather than striking at the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 c5 5.cxd5.strategy: Resolves the tension in the centre at once. After the recapture White can drive the knight away with e4, which the pawn on f3 supports, and fight for a broad centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 c5 5.dxc5.strategy: Takes the pawn and gives up the d4 pawn's grip on the centre. But Black regains it with ...Qa5, which pins the c3 knight against the king and attacks c5, and then plays against a loosened centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 c5 5.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop, a solid way to meet the strike at the centre. But White has now spent two moves on pawns in front of the kingside pieces, and the knight has lost its natural square on f3; Black can trade on d4 or take on c4 and play comfortably.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 c5 5.cxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, centralising it and attacking the c3 knight. Together with the pawn on c5 hitting d4, Black has pressure on the centre at once, and White's plan of building it with e4 has to be paid for.
Hangs the queen: the c3 knight takes it, and Black gets only a knight in return.

Recaptures on d4 first, but 6.Qxd4 leaves White a pawn up. The d5 pawn is attacked twice and defended twice, so ...Nxd5 loses material to the exchanges that follow, and Black has to spend time to win the pawn back.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 c5 5.cxd5.name: Grünfeld Defence: Lutikov Variation, Murrey Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 c5 5.cxd5.background: A modified version of Ashot Nadanian's idea of Na4, it has been called the Neo-Nadanian.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.f3 c5 5.cxd5.strategy: Attacks the c5 pawn a second time: with d4 and the knight on it, and nothing guarding it, Black must resolve the tension at once. The knight stands on the edge, but the move gains a tempo.

Drives the d5 knight away with the pawn on f3 behind it and builds the broad centre this set-up is designed for. White gains space and the initiative for now. The cost is that the centre becomes a target: the c5 pawn already presses on d4 and the bishop will join it.
Takes the pawn, but it is hard to keep: ...Qa5 pins the c3 knight against the king and attacks c5, and Black wins the pawn back with active play against a centre that no longer has its d-pawn.
